awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I:  A Platform for Penetrative Drug Delivery to Teeth
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is a novel medical device and dental approach for enabling rapid and more effective dental treatments by improving the permeability of pharmaceuticals and cosmetics into teeth. The system aims to augment the delivery of specific compounds for treating tooth decay resulting in over 175 million cavities drilled and filled and $45 billion costs per year in the US, with nearly 15 million requiring root canal therapy resulting in $15 billion costs to remove the underlying infection which topical or systemic antibiotics are unable to effectively treat. In the short term, the system aims to provide an augmentative method for the cosmetic dentistry market by improving teeth whitening treatments currently performed by nearly 80% of Americans, a $7 billion market when combining both the professional and over-the-counter whitening treatment markets. 


This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project seeks to validate a novel device and approach for controlling electrically-mediated electrokinetic flow for enhancing the delivery of pharmaceuticals and cosmetics into whole human teeth. The novel system is based on experimental results demonstrating electrical voltage, current, time of application, pressure, with an additive for maintaining conductivity improves permeability of specific chemical formulations. These parameters will be validated on the speed and depth of delivery and their effects characterized using several commonly topically applied dental agents including fluoride and hydrogen peroxide bleach. Isolated invitro testing will then be completed to expand the potential for several relevant molecules including antimicrobial and regenerative agents. A prototype device will then be fabricated for enabling first in-human testing at a latter stage. The successful completion of this project therefore aims to demonstrate the technical feasibility of a novel approach for enabling deeper and more rapid delivery of several clinically relevant molecules into human teeth in an invitro setting, and completion of a prototype device suitable for experimental use.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Overview and Intellectual Merit:

This Phase I project investigated a new, non-invasive approach for delivering therapeutic substances into teeth using a low-energy electrical process. Tooth decay (also known as dental caries or cavities) is one of the most prevalent chronic diseases worldwide and is most often treated through drilling and filling, which removes healthy tooth structure and can lead to repeated restorative procedures over a patient's lifetime. Many existing dental treatments, such as fluoride rinses or antimicrobial gels, primarily act on the tooth surface and have limited ability to reach deeper regions where disease can progress.

During the project, the research team demonstrated that multiple well-established dental therapeutic agents could be delivered through intact human tooth tissue. Experiments were conducted on extracted human teeth and measured delivery only after agents had fully traversed enamel and dentin, the hard mineralized layers of the tooth. This conservative testing approach ensured that results reflected true penetration rather than surface coating. Under these conditions, therapeutic agents were shown to pass through approximately two millimeters of enamel and dentin in under ten minutes.

The team quantitatively measured delivery rates for several classes of dental therapeutics, including fluoride (used to prevent cavities), chlorhexidine (a common dental antimicrobial), hydrogen peroxide (used for whitening and antimicrobial activity), and potassium (used to reduce tooth sensitivity). Measured delivery rates were compared to published biological benchmarks to assess whether the amounts delivered were plausibly sufficient to produce known biological effects. Across all tested agents, delivery levels were consistent with ranges associated with cavity prevention, bacterial growth suppression, and nerve desensitization, even under conservative test conditions.

In addition, the project demonstrated that delivery could be actively controlled by adjusting electrical parameters. By varying applied voltage, the research team showed predictable changes in delivery rate, establishing a foundation for tunable dose control. This ability to modulate delivery without changing the therapeutic substance itself represents a key scientific advance and de-risks the platform for future development. Together, these results advance fundamental understanding of transport through mineralized tissues and establish a quantitative framework for controlled, non-invasive delivery into teeth.

Broader Impacts:

The broader impacts of this work include the potential to reduce reliance on invasive dental procedures by enabling therapeutic agents to reach deeper regions of the tooth without drilling. Such approaches could help preserve healthy tooth structure, improve patient comfort, and support earlier intervention for tooth decay and sensitivity. Non-invasive treatment options may be particularly beneficial for children, older adults, individuals with dental anxiety, and populations with limited access to routine dental care.

Beyond dentistry, this project contributes new methods for studying and benchmarking delivery through hard biological materials, which may inform future research in biomedical engineering and materials science. The project also supported interdisciplinary training at the interface of engineering, chemistry, and dental science, helping to develop a workforce skilled in translational medical device research. Overall, this Phase I effort established a strong scientific foundation for continued research and development toward practical, patient-centered dental therapies.
